The CFO job has gone from accountant to banker to builder, and the whole finance function is being rebuilt around it:

1. Data stopped being the bottleneck. AI pulls and reconciles data across systems, so teams spend more time acting on numbers instead of chasing them.

2. The finance stack is becoming part of the finance team. AI-native tools stand up in days, pull their own data, and turn a monthly close into a daily one.

3. The rise of the finance engineer. Finance people proficient in Claude Code or Codex are building their own tools.

4. The finance team gets smaller and higher leverage. The old heuristic of finance at 5% of headcount is heading to 2% for the leanest teams.

5. Planning becomes continuous. Usage-based revenue (tokens, API calls) moves too fast for a monthly forecast, so planning shifts from annual budgets to a live view.

6. Controls become a critical feature of the product. Every number an agent touches keeps an audit trail back to its source, and finance still owns sign-off.

7. Finance gets a bigger mandate. Compute spend, people versus software, and build versus buy are now finance decisions.

"The CFO is becoming a builder and architect of the company's operating system... The job is still finance, but more of the job now is designing how finance gets done."

ICYMI, last week I compared @worldnetwork and @Concordium’s different approaches to private identity.

This week I went through some of their docs, and I found a few more things that make those differences a bit clearer when it comes to AI agents.

World starts with proof of personhood. A verified human can delegate their World ID to an agent, proving that a real, unique human sits behind it. That’s especially useful for Sybil resistance.

Concordium $CCD approaches the problem differently:

Its Agent Registry gives the agent its own onchain identity anchor, linked to the verified human or business behind it. Each agent can also carry a declared scope of what it's authorised to do, recorded onchain.

That’s an essential distinction.

Once agents start holding wallets, making payments, and acting independently, knowing that a human exists somewhere behind the agent isn’t the whole problem.

You also need to know who stands behind that specific agent, what it is authorised to do, and who is accountable when it acts.

And all of that needs to happen without publicly exposing the identity underneath.

I think the agent economy is shifting from proof of personhood to proof of accountability.

The signs are everywhere.

How fud goes in crypto:

- It lands when coins already wanted to roll over. The chart was weak and the fud takes the blame.

- The most potent fud is the kind nobody can verify. Right now no one can tell you whether AI can break elliptic curves, or when. You can't prove it. You can't rule it out either. That's what gives it legs.

- The shock hits. People panic and timelines fill up with worst case engagement farming.

- Over the next few days the sensible takes arrive. Logic wins and the world doesn't end.

- Price ends up where it was going anyway. The only real change is that people who blasted the highs capitulate. 

None of this means the risk is zero. It means the market reaction follows a script, and the script tells you almost nothing about the risk itself.

The sensible take is that the same maths secures the whole internet. Banking, messaging, every HTTPS connection. If a break were imminent, the people with the best information would be in emergency mode. They're not.
